notes: Tagged repository baseline euro-2028-baseline remains contract 63. Contracts 64–100 establish the multi-competition season foundations, domestic game engines, Cup-neutral sources, provider custody and the two tournament-path corrections. Contract 101 removes obsolete shared-league gating from Euro post-lock reveal without widening pre-lock access. Contract 102 persists the Predictor Championship split as a distinct phase. Contract 103 reconciles game availability with repeatable competition instances: one live public row per season game, one live row per independent series, public/private coexistence, scoped predecessor lineage and bounded completion reasons. Contract 104 keeps five operational callers live-only and moves five read surfaces onto a current-public resolver that prefers live and otherwise retains the latest terminal result; Contract 102 Cup phase filters remain intact. Contract 105 enforces one-parent split ancestry and derives the continuing Championship table from settled initial and split fixtures without copying a starting total. Contract 107 is the Last Man Standing restart itself: it completes a wiped-out competition as no_winner_restarted, creates one linked successor, re-enters every entrant and copies no selections, cycles, projections or windows. Contract 108 guards the gap that deferral leaves — a successor may not hold a round that opened or locked before its predecessor finished, so the catalogue publisher cannot give a fresh competition rounds nobody could play in. Contract 109 closes the deferral itself: the next eligible league round is derived from the existing matchweek lock authority, the successor's calendar is generated from it exactly once, and an hourly job drives the restart from what settlement reported. Settlement continues only to derive and report. Contract 110 gives the season Predictor Championship rounds it can be played over: until it, nothing in the repository created a window for a season competition while bonus_cup_fixtures.window_id is NOT NULL, so no season Championship fixture could be persisted in either phase. It schedules N rounds from the next eligible league matchweeks, refuses a season that cannot supply the whole format rather than truncating it, and appends rather than owning the calendar so the split phase can be scheduled on the same competition later. Contract 111 launches a season Championship: threshold, format, initial group, draw, rounds and round-robin fixtures. It drives the single-group shape and refuses the multi-group one by name. The public threshold applies only to public competitions — a hundred-entrant field always takes the multi-group shape, so the shape this drives belongs to organiser-created private competitions. Hosted deployment remains separately guarded and is not claimed by this repository contract. Contract 114 gives the season matchweek card its bounded browser path: one read and three writes scoped to the caller's own entry, with locks, the Joker allowance and version conflicts enforced by the triggers that already own them, a version column and PT409 trigger on season_predictions, and the delete path brought under the matchweek lock so clearing a prediction or taking back a Joker after lock refuses. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 115 makes the database able to call out at all: it installs pg_net, forbids any browser-reachable function in an exposed schema from calling into net, and drives the deployed provider-poll Edge Function from pg_cron at the cadence each target declares. pg_net's own grants belong to whoever owns the extension — where Supabase's image owns it, postgres is neither superuser nor a member of supabase_admin and cannot revoke them, which CI established by refusing the first version of the migration rather than by review. It records no poll target and imports no fixture, so on application the job runs and does nothing. Contract 116 lets a season Last Man Standing entrant SEE the round they can already pick in: contract 86 widened the selection trigger to season fixtures but the READ was never widened, so get_my_lms resolves every window through bonus_window_fixtures joined to public.matches and returns a season round with an empty fixture array. get_season_lms_round reads season_cup_window_fixtures joined to season_fixtures instead, and returns the survival verdict from predictor_internal.season_lms_pick_outcome — the same authority the settlement replay folds over — rather than handing a browser raw scores to judge, because a season fixture carries no winner column. It returns one round, the earliest still open to a pick, and nothing about any other entrant. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 117 is the repeatable path a provider kickoff change takes to the fixture: it revises an existing kickoff, creates none, deletes none and never writes competition_round_id, which is the owner amendment made executable. It fails closed on the whole payload when any identifier is unmapped, refuses a kickoff moved into the past and a fixture no longer scheduled, and records every move append-only as an administrator review queue. Contract 118 stops the games hub being blind to a season's fixtures: get_bonus_games built its per-window fixtures from bonus_window_fixtures joined to public.matches with no branch on competition kind, so a season window returned an empty array — and because resolveCompetitionStatus can only settle a window when total > 0 and confirmed >= total, a season competition's first locked round stayed in flight permanently and the hub card stuck on it. Three internal functions supply the facts instead: a tournament limb, a season limb mapping season status onto the tournament vocabulary on contract 77's established equivalence, and a neutral combiner that unions rather than branches because a window's fixtures live in exactly one source. get_bonus_games is redefined from contract 104's text with only its fixtures subquery changed, verified by diff rather than by reading. This is the fourth instance of one defect — contracts 86, 98, 116 and this — and 168_tournament_only_browser_reads.sql now catches the fifth; get_bonus_games leaves that list by earning its removal. No table grant is added, no browser function is added, and no rule moves. Contract 119 makes a rescheduled fixture lock at its own kickoff. Contract 117 let a provider move a kickoff automatically and the lock did not follow, so a fixture postponed to the following Wednesday still locked on Saturday. Only a rescheduled fixture is affected — the owner chose that reading over the universal per-fixture one, which shares the same arithmetic but would make an ordinary matchweek predictable in stages. "Moved" is contract 117's revision record, a stored fact rather than an inference, and the rule is strictly permissive: it can extend an editing window, never shorten one. Contract 120 gives the Predictor Championship's phase and continuing table a bounded browser read. Contract 102 persists the split as a distinct phase and contract 105 derives its continuing table, and no browser-reachable function read either — measured on hosted development, zero functions authenticated may execute read cup_split_group_tables, parent_group_id or cup_final_group_tables, and get_my_cup was last defined on 29 July 2026, before the split phase existed. Fifth instance of the contract 86/98/116/118 defect, along the initial-versus-split axis rather than the tournament-versus-season one. get_season_cup_phase returns the caller's own phase and their own group's table from whichever authority owns that phase: cup_split_group_tables already filters phase_kind = 'split', so the branch is a lookup of an established fact rather than a new decision. It adds no rule, recomputes nothing, joins no profile, and gives a non-entrant entered=false rather than an exception. Contract 121 gives a season's play context: which season a URL means, and which matchweek its card opens at. Registering the UI-04 surface needed two facts the browser cannot obtain. The slug lives in public.competitions, which is revoked from every browser role and returned by no function, and two seasons sharing a season_key are told apart only by competition_id — the column pointing at the table the browser cannot read; (competitions.slug, tournaments.season_key) is a real composite key because both are unique. Contract 114's read then takes the matchweek as an argument and nothing told the caller what to pass; public.competition_rounds is revoked from the browser, so a client cannot derive it either, and deriving it in JavaScript would put a second answer beside the one the database owns. Nothing new is decided: predictor_internal.next_eligible_league_round already answers this for the Last Man Standing successor scheduler, ordering by the DERIVED lock instant rather than by ordinal so a rescheduled season resolves to the round that actually locks next — the property contract 119 made matter. This exposes that answer and adds no scheduling logic. It returns no prediction, entry, standing or other player, so it is not gated on an entry; a season past its last lock reports a null matchweek as an ordinary end-of-season state, while an unknown competition or a tournament-shaped one raises, because a single null for both would let a typo read as a finished season. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 122 makes the two retention tables ADR 0012 names answerable at last: monthlyStandings and rollingFormPoints have existed in src/domain/season/standings.ts since contract 94 and were called by nothing. Both are derived views over settled matchweek totals and neither writes a score, a standing or a settlement — the cumulative total remains the only ranking that decides a season. A matchweek belongs to exactly one month because season_matchweek_scores is keyed per matchweek and never per fixture, so the only question is which instant names it: the round's window_opens_at, read in the competition's own display_timezone, because a month boundary is not a UTC fact and a 23:30Z kickoff on 31 July is August in Europe/London. An unplaceable settled matchweek refuses the whole monthly table rather than misranking a month, mirroring the TypeScript's null. Form needs no calendar at all — most-recent is an order, and competition_rounds.ordinal already carries it — so it answers on a season whose windows were never derived. The migration also runs contract 113's derive_round_play_windows once per league season, which nothing had ever called, leaving every window null. Keeping them fresh is deliberately NOT added: exactly one function moves a season kickoff, contract 117's provider import, and re-deriving after it could make an ordinary import start failing when a postponed fixture extends a round's span into the next round's, which contract 113's disjointness trigger refuses. That is a behaviour change to ingestion rather than to a standings view, so it stays an owner decision.
